The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Great London Plane of Ely
Platanus × acerifolia
The broad-canopied witness of open sky and stone.

NATURAL HISTORY
London plane is a vigorous hybrid tree, long valued in towns, parks and avenues. Its patchwork bark peels in plates to reveal pale green, cream and olive beneath, while broad maple-like leaves and hanging seed-balls mark the seasons. It can grow immense, casting a spacious canopy that feels both civic and sheltering.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
A mature plane offers shade, roosting places and refuge for urban wildlife. Rough bark, old cavities and branch architecture create niches for insects, lichens and birds, while fallen leaves feed the living soil below. In open landscapes it becomes a gathering tree — a living roof for meeting, rest, play and quiet thought.

TRADITIONS & LORE
Plane trees have long been planted where people gather: beside roads, in commons, near schools and along public walks. They are trees of welcome, endurance and civic memory — companions to conversation and crossing. The Great London Plane of Ely stands in that tradition, joining rooted strength with an open, generous presence.

A REFLECTION
Wide-limbed and weather-bright, the Plane
holds a room beneath the sky.
Its bark remembers change without losing form,
and its shade invites the world to draw near.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
Where in your life are you being asked
to stand broad, open and sheltering?

Plane leaf and seed-balls

The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Holly
Ilex aquifolium
The evergreen that holds the winter.

NATURAL HISTORY
Holly is a native tree of Britain, found in woodlands, hedgerows and ancient landscapes. It can live for hundreds of years, reaching 10–20 metres, often as a tree or a dense, sheltering shrub. Its glossy, spiny leaves and bright red berries make it one of the most recognisable trees in our winter world.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
Holly is a vital winter resource. Its berries feed birds such as blackbird, thrush, robin and waxwing when other food is scarce. Its dense, evergreen cover offers shelter and nesting places, and its spring flowers provide nectar and pollen for bees and other pollinators. Holly helps to keep woodland edges rich and resilient.

TRADITIONS & LORE
In Celtic tradition, Holly was a tree of protection, renewal and life through winter. It was hung in homes to bring good fortune and keep away harm, and often paired with Ivy as a symbol of balance — light and dark, rest and return. Its ever-living leaves remind us that life continues, even when the land seems to sleep.

A REFLECTION
Among bare branches, Holly stands green,
a quiet flame in the winter’s breath.
It shelters, feeds and keeps the promise
that life endures, and will return.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
What does the living world keep alive
through the darker days?

IMAGE CAPTIONS
Holly flowers (Spring)
Holly berries (Winter)

companions.learningNote: Evergreen holly shelters wildlife. Its berries feed birds but are harmful if eaten by people. Real holly flowers typically have four petals. Heights and bird visitors vary; the foliage and flower details here are stylised. The reference to ‘Celtic tradition’ is unverified folklore.

The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Yarrow
Achillea millefolium
The field herb that gathers healing light.

NATURAL HISTORY
Yarrow is a hardy perennial of meadows, paths and open ground. Its finely divided, feather-like leaves and flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers make it one of the most recognisable wild herbs of summer. It spreads by root and seed, returning year after year with a quiet, enduring presence.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
Yarrow is a generous plant for pollinators, drawing bees, hoverflies, beetles and butterflies to its many small florets. It thrives in lean soils and sunny places, helping weave resilient meadow communities. Its long flowering season makes it a faithful bridge between abundance and decline.

TRADITIONS & LORE
Linked in legend to Achilles, Yarrow has long been associated with mending and protection. It has been used in herbal traditions for wounds, boundaries and blessing, and has also appeared in folklore as a plant of divination and steadfast love. It carries an old memory of healing close at hand.

A REFLECTION
Feather-leaved and many-flowered,
Yarrow keeps the memory of repair.
It gathers small lives around it, and
teaches that healing is often humble,
patient and near.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
What in you is ready to mend,
gather and rejoin the whole?

IMAGE CAPTIONS
Yarrow flowers
Feathery leaf detail

companions.learningNote: Yarrow is a meadow perennial with finely divided leaves and many tiny flowers. The healing language here describes poetry and traditional associations, not a medical recommendation.

reverse.readableText:
The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Coco de Mer
Lodoicea maldivica
The giant seed that carries an island mystery.

NATURAL HISTORY
Coco de mer is an extraordinary palm found naturally only in the Seychelles. Its immense double-lobed seed is the largest in the plant kingdom, and the tree itself grows slowly, taking many years to flower and fruit. Separate male and female trees shape one of the most remarkable life cycles in the botanical world.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
This great palm belongs to ancient island forests, where moisture, shade and time all matter. Its broad leaves help shape the forest floor, and its rare seeds speak of a habitat that cannot be hurried. Coco de mer reminds us that some forms of life depend on patience, protection and ecological wholeness.

TRADITIONS & LORE
Before its true home was known, coco de mer seeds were found floating at sea and were once believed to come from trees growing beneath the ocean. The seed became a marvel of trade, story and imagination, and today iit stands as an emblem of rarity and wonder — a treasure best honoured through care rather than possession.

A REFLECTION
Immense and tidal-shaped, Coco de Mer
asks for a slower measure of value.
It teaches that what is rare and ancient
is not ours to seize, but ours to protect.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
How do you care for what is rare,
slow and irreplaceable?

IMAGE CAPTIONS
Giant seed detail
Palm frond

companions.learningNote: The living palm has large fan-shaped leaves; the painting stylises its fronds. Its double-lobed seed is distinct from the surrounding fruit. Viable seeds are too dense to float like coconuts; stories of drifting material are not a dispersal guide.

The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Field Maple
Acer campestre
The hedgerow leaf that turns the margins gold.

NATURAL HISTORY
Field Maple is Britain’s native maple, most often found in hedgerows, woodland edges and old field boundaries. It is a modest tree, yet full of grace, with small five-lobed leaves, neat branching and paired winged seeds. In autumn it turns cleat yellow and amber, lighting quiet margins with colour.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
Field Maple supports many insects and offers shelter for birds within thick hedges and mixed countryside edges. Its flowers feed pollinators in spring, and its leaves and seeds become part of the wider web of seasonal exchange. It is a tree of connected places — lanes, fields, gardens and village greens.

TRADITIONS & LORE
Though less celebrated than oak or ash, Field Maple has long belonged to the lived texture of rural life. It is a tree of boundaries, craft and everyday beauty, often woven into hedge-lines and farmed landscapes. Its gift is not grandeur but companionship — a native presence that belongs by staying near.

A REFLECTION
Small in stature and bright in turning,
Field Maple keeps the beauty of the edge.
It teaches that quiet places, faithfully held,
can glow with their own importance.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
What quiet edge in your life is asking
to be noticed and valued?

IMAGE CAPTIONS
Field Maple flowers (Spring)
Autumn leaf
Winged seeds (Samaras)

companions.learningNote: Field maple, Acer campestre, has five blunt, rounded lobes and rounded teeth. The leaf and insets have been corrected while retaining the Holly frame. The printed “cleat yellow” should read “clear yellow”.

The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Ivy Blossom
Hedera helix
The late flower that keeps the season open.

NATURAL HISTORY
Ivy is an evergreen climber and woodland companion, but its flowering phase is one of the quiet wonders of autumn. When many plants are fading, Ivy lifts pale green-yellow flower clusters into the late light. Its glossy leaves, wandering stems and seasonal transformation make it both familiar and full of surprise.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
Ivy blossom is one of the most valuable late nectar sources for bees, hoverflies and wasps, and its berries later feed birds through winter. Dense ivy cover also offers nesting shelter and refuge. It stands at the turning of the year, feeding life when other doors are closing.

TRADITIONS & LORE
In folklore, Ivy has long symbolised endurance, fidelity and the power of life to persist through dark seasons. It is often paired with Holly as a balancing companion — evergreen with evergreen, shelter with shelter. Ivy teaches the strength of climbing, clinging and quietly remaining.

A REFLECTION
Late-flowering and ever-climbing,
Ivy keeps the season open. It reminds us
that life does not end where summer fades;
it gathers itself and offers again.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
Where is life still flowering in you —
late, faithful and full of offering?

IMAGE CAPTIONS
Ivy flowers
Glossy leaf detail

companions.learningNote: Ivy has two leaf forms: juvenile shoots usually bear lobed leaves; mature flowering shoots bear unlobed leaves. This painting combines the stages.

reverse.readableText:
The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Blueberries
Vaccinium spp.
The blue fruit that gathers summer into sweetness.

NATURAL HISTORY
Blueberries belong to the Vaccinium family, a group of shrubs known for their bell-shaped flowers and dusky blue fruits. They thrive best in acidic soils and bright, open places, whether in woodland clearings, moorland kinlands or cultivated gardens. Their fruit carries both freshness and depth, ripening slowly into summer sweetness.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
Blueberries feed bees when in flower and later nourish birds, mammals and people with their abundant berries. Their shrubs offer cover close to the ground, and their fruiting ties together pollinators, foragers and seed-dispersers. They are a reminder that sweetness is part of ecology, not apart from it.

TRADITIONS & LORE
Blue fruits have long belonged to summer gathering, preserving and sharing. Whether eaten fresh, baked, dried or made into jam, blueberries carry a sense of abundance held in small form. They belong to the basket, the path and the berry-stained hand — gifts of season, memory and delight.

A REFLECTION
Round and blue with gathered light,
Blueberries ripen by degrees.
They teach that sweetness often arrives
quietly, one small fruit at a time.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
What sweetness is ripening quietly
in your life?

IMAGE CAPTIONS
Berry cluster
Leaf detail

companions.learningNote: Blueberries belong to the genus Vaccinium, in the family Ericaceae. This companion represents blueberries at genus level, not an identified cultivar or species. The printed ‘Vaccinium family’ is incorrect; ‘moorland kinlands’ is a wording error.

reverse.readableText:
The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Turkey Tail
Trametes versicolor
The layered fan that returns wood to earth.

NATURAL HISTORY
Turkey Tail is a thin, shelf-like bracket fungus found on fallen branches, stumps and decaying logs. Its many bands of brown, grey, cream and rust give it the look of layered feathers, which is how it earned its name. It is common, beautiful and easy to overlook until one kneels close to the wood.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
As a white-rot fungus, Turkey Tail helps break down wood and return its matter to the living system. It turns fallen timber into habitat, food and soil, opening space for insects, mosses, microbes and future growth. It is one of the quiet recyclers that keeps woodland cycles moving.

TRADITIONS & LORE
Turkey Tail has become one of the most widely recognised medicinal fungi in modern herbal and mycological conversation, while its patterned bands have long inspired simple wonder. It teaches that beauty often appears in the work of decay, and that endings can be richly inhabited.

A REFLECTION
Layer upon layer, Turkey Tail opens on
fallen wood like a patient fan. It reminds
us that what is breaking down may also
be feeding what comes next.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
What in your life is ready to
become soil for new growth?

IMAGE CAPTIONS
Bracket layers
Pore underside detail

companions.learningNote: Turkey Tail recycles dead wood and has fine pores underneath. The enlarged underside detail is stylised. ‘Medicinal’ here refers to traditional associations and research, not a treatment or an identification/edibility claim.

The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Return of the Bird Tribes
Ken Carey
A visionary book of remembrance and kinship.

ABOUT THE BOOK
Return of the Bird Tribes is a visionary work by Ken Carey that speaks in a lyrical, prophetic voice about humanity, consciousness and the living Earth. It invites the reader to step beyond ordinary habit and remember a more sacred relationship with the world. The book feels less like an argument and more like a summons.

THEMES & GIFTS
Awakening, imagination, service and reverence run through the book like bright threads. Birds appear as messengers of perspective, migration and soul-memory, carrying the sense that another way of being human is still possible. It is a text that asks not only to be read, but listened to.

COUNCIL & CONNECTIONS
For the Council of Life, this book offers companionship in the work of remembering kinship with creation. It speaks to those who feel that culture can turn again toward humility, wonder and participation in a larger living order. Its gift is to re-open the conversation between spirit, Earth and responsibility.

A REFLECTION
Some books do not simply inform; they call.
Return of the Bird Tribes opens a skyward path,

ABOUT THE BOOK
Return of the Bird Tribes is a visionary work by Ken Carey that speaks in a lyrical, prophetic voice about humanity, consciousness and the living Earth. It invites the reader to step beyond ordinary habit and remember a more sacred relationship with the world. The book feels less like an argument and more like a summons.

THEMES & GIFTS
Awakening, imagination, service and reverence run through the book like bright threads. Birds appear as messengers of perspective, migration and soul-memory, carrying the sense that another way of being human is still possible. It is a text that asks not only to be read, but listened to.

COUNCIL & CONNECTIONS
For the Council of Life, this book offers companionship in the work of remembering kinship with creation. It speaks to those who feel that culture can turn again toward humility, wonder and participation in a larger living order. Its gift is to re-open the conversation between spirit, Earth and responsibility.

reverse.readableText:
The Council of Life
CIRCLE 242 · 23–29 NOVEMBER 2026

Barn Owl
Tyto alba
The pale-winged hunter of dusk and meadow.

NATURAL HISTORY
Barn Owl is one of Britain’s most recognisable birds of prey, known for its pale plumage, heart-shaped face and almost silent flight. It hunts mainly at dusk and after dark, quartering meadows and rough grass for voles and other small mammals. It nests in barns, towers, tree cavities and other quiet sheltered places.

ECOLOGY & CONNECTIONS
Barn Owls depend on rich grassland habitats, hedgerows and field margins that hold abundant prey. Their pellets tell the story of local small-mammal life, making them messengers of place as well as hunters within it. Where Barn Owls thrive, a whole web of rough meadow life is often still intact.

TRADITIONS & LORE
In folklore, Barn Owls have often been seen as ghost-birds, night-watchers or omens, their pale forms drifting through the dark. Yet they also carry another meaning: stillness, precision and listening. They belong to the threshold between fear and wonder, reminding us that the night is full of presence.

A REFLECTION
Soft-winged and lantern-faced, the Barn Owl
moves through dusk with still attention.
It teaches that there is a way of knowing
that comes not by noise, but by listening.

THE COUNCIL QUESTION [printed heading; this is a companion invitation, not a separate weekly inquiry]
What helps you listen more deeply
and move with grace through the dark?
